notes.front: What is accountability, as a security goal?
notes.back: The goal that requires the actions of an entity to be traced uniquely to that entity.
notes.explanation: NIST states it as a security goal that creates a requirement: every action must be traceable to exactly one entity.
notes.example: Like a signed delivery note that shows which driver dropped off each parcel, but for every action on a system, recorded against one named account.
notes.evidence: Accountability The security goal that generates the requirement for actions of an entity to be traced uniquely to that entity.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1, Appendix B Glossary, “Accountability”, p. 86

notes.front: What are rules of behaviour?
notes.back: Rules given to everyone who needs access to a system, describing their responsibilities and expected behaviour for its use, security and privacy.
notes.explanation: NIST's rules-of-behaviour control also requires a documented acknowledgement from each person, saying they have read, understood and agreed to the rules, before access is authorised.
notes.example: Like the house rules a gym member signs before getting a key fob, but covering how staff may use the organisation's systems and data.
notes.evidence: Establish and provide to individuals requiring access to the system, the rules that describe their responsibilities and expected behavior for information and system usage, security, and privacy;
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, PL-4 Rules of Behavior, p. 224

notes.front: Tracing actions to the entity that performed them supports which other aims? Name two.
notes.back: Any two of: non-repudiation; deterrence; fault isolation; intrusion detection and prevention; after-action recovery and legal action.
notes.explanation: NIST's definition of accountability lists these as the things the goal supports.
notes.evidence: This supports nonrepudiation, deterrence, fault isolation, intrusion detection and This publication is available free of charge from: https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-12r1 prevention, and after-action recovery and legal action.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1, Appendix B Glossary, “Accountability”, p. 86

notes.front: Accountability requires the actions of an entity to be traced {{c1::uniquely}} to that entity.
notes.back: uniquely
notes.explanation: If an action could belong to more than one entity, the trace no longer meets NIST's definition of accountability.
notes.evidence: the requirement for actions of an entity to be traced uniquely to that entity.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1, Appendix B Glossary, “Accountability”, p. 86

notes.front: A network team wants every firewall rule change to be traceable to the engineer who made it. Which arrangement meets that goal?
notes.back: Each engineer makes changes through an individual, named account.
notes.choices:
A) One shared administrator account with a strong password
B) Individual named accounts for each engineer
C) A shared account whose password changes every week
D) A shared account used only from one jump server
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and D: with any shared account, a change can be tied only to the account, not uniquely to one engineer, however well the account is protected.
notes.explanation: Accountability requires each action to be traced uniquely to the entity that performed it, which a shared account cannot give.
notes.evidence: the requirement for actions of an entity to be traced uniquely to that entity.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1, Appendix B Glossary, “Accountability”, p. 86

notes.front: What forms can a documented acknowledgement of rules of behaviour take?
notes.back: Electronic or physical signatures, and electronic agreement check boxes or radio buttons.
notes.explanation: The control asks for a documented acknowledgement, and its discussion names these as acceptable ways to record it.
notes.evidence: Documented acknowledgements for rules of behavior include electronic or physical signatures and electronic agreement check boxes or radio buttons.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, PL-4 Rules of Behavior, Discussion, p. 224

notes.front: Should privileged users and general users get the same rules of behaviour?
notes.back: Not necessarily: organisations base the rules on roles and responsibilities and distinguish rules for privileged users from rules for general users.
notes.explanation: The control's discussion ties the rules to each person's role, so an administrator's rules can differ from a clerk's.
notes.evidence: Organizations consider rules of behavior based on individual user roles and responsibilities and differentiate between rules that apply to privileged users and rules that apply to general users.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, PL-4 Rules of Behavior, Discussion, p. 224

notes.front: The social media enhancement to rules of behaviour adds restrictions on which activities? Name two.
notes.back: Any two of: using social media and external sites; posting organisational information publicly; creating external accounts with work identifiers and passwords.
notes.explanation: The social media enhancement lists these three restrictions for the organisation to include in its rules.
notes.evidence: Include in the rules of behavior, restrictions on: (a) Use of social media, social networking sites, and external sites/applications; (b) Posting organizational information on public websites; and (c) Use of organization-provided identifiers (e.g., email addresses) and authentication secrets (e.g., passwords) for creating accounts on external sites/applications.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, PL-4(1) Social Media and External Site/Application Usage Restrictions, p. 224

notes.front: An engineer signs up for a free online diagram tool using his work email address and the same password he uses at work. Which part of the organisation's rules of behaviour should cover this?
notes.back: The restriction on using organisation-provided identifiers and authentication secrets to create accounts on external sites.
notes.choices:
A) The restriction on using work identifiers and passwords for external accounts
B) The requirement to review and update the rules periodically
C) The rule that access is authorised only after acknowledgement
D) The restriction on posting organisational information on public websites
notes.choicesExplained: B: the review cycle concerns the organisation keeping the rules current, not this behaviour. C: he already has access; the issue is what he did with his credentials. D: he posted nothing; he created an account.
notes.explanation: The social media enhancement names exactly this: using organisation-provided identifiers such as email addresses and secrets such as passwords to create external accounts.
notes.evidence: Use of organization-provided identifiers (e.g., email addresses) and authentication secrets (e.g., passwords) for creating accounts on external sites/applications.

notes.front: Non-repudiation protects against which false claims? Name two.
notes.back: Any two of: an author denying authorship; a sender denying sending; a receiver denying receipt; a signatory denying signing.
notes.explanation: NIST's non-repudiation control lists these four denials as what the service protects against.
notes.evidence: Non-repudiation protects against claims by authors of not having authored certain documents, senders of not having transmitted messages, receivers of not having received messages, and signatories of not having signed documents.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, AU-10 Non-repudiation, Discussion, p. 103

notes.front: Accountability versus non-repudiation: how are they related?
notes.back: Accountability is the goal of tracing each action uniquely to its entity; non-repudiation is one of the things that goal supports.
notes.explanation: NIST's definition of accountability names non-repudiation first among the aims it supports, so the tracing comes first and the proof against denial builds on it.
notes.evidence: The security goal that generates the requirement for actions of an entity to be traced uniquely to that entity. This supports nonrepudiation,
notes.source: NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1, Appendix B Glossary, “Accountability”, p. 86

notes.front: A supplier insists it never received a purchase order. The buyer produces a digital message receipt showing the supplier's system accepted it. Which property does the receipt provide?
notes.back: Non-repudiation: evidence against the receiver's claim of not having received the message.
notes.choices:
A) Availability
B) Confidentiality
C) Non-repudiation
D) Integrity
notes.choicesExplained: A: the question is not whether the order system was usable. B: nothing was disclosed. D: nobody claims the order was altered; the dispute is whether it was received.
notes.explanation: NIST lists digital message receipts among the mechanisms for non-repudiation, which protects against receivers claiming they never received a message.
notes.evidence: Organizations obtain nonrepudiation services by employing various techniques or mechanisms, including digital signatures and digital message receipts.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, AU-10 Non-repudiation, Discussion, p. 103

notes.front: Under NIST's least privilege controls, what account should an administrator use for everyday non-security work?
notes.back: A non-privileged account or role.
notes.explanation: The enhancement says using non-privileged accounts for non-security functions limits exposure when operating from privileged accounts.
notes.evidence: Requiring the use of non-privileged accounts when accessing nonsecurity functions limits exposure when operating from within privileged accounts or roles.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, AC-6(2) Non-privileged Access for Nonsecurity Functions, p. 64

notes.front: Why does NIST's least privilege control ask for the use of privileged functions to be logged?
notes.back: Logging and analysing it is one way to detect misuse of privileged functions.
notes.explanation: The control says detecting such misuse helps mitigate the risk from insider threats and the advanced persistent threat.
notes.evidence: Logging and analyzing the use of privileged functions is one way to detect such misuse and, in doing so, help mitigate the risk from insider threats and the advanced persistent threat.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, AC-6(9) Log Use of Privileged Functions, p. 65

notes.front: Which functions count as privileged functions in NIST's least privilege control? Name two.
notes.back: Any two of: disabling, circumventing or altering security or privacy controls; establishing system accounts; performing system integrity checks; administering cryptographic key management.
notes.explanation: The control says non-privileged users must be prevented from executing these, and its discussion lists them as examples.
notes.evidence: Privileged functions include disabling, circumventing, or altering implemented security or privacy controls, establishing system accounts, performing system integrity checks, and administering cryptographic key management activities.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, AC-6(10) Prohibit Non-privileged Users from Executing Privileged Functions, p. 65

notes.front: A domain administrator reads email and browses supplier websites all day while signed in to her domain administrator account. What does least privilege call for?
notes.back: She should use a separate non-privileged account for email and browsing, and the privileged one only for security functions.
notes.choices:
A) Keep one account but have its activity logged
B) Remove her administrator rights altogether
C) Give her a shared administrator account instead
D) Use a non-privileged account for everyday work
notes.choicesExplained: A: logging helps detect misuse but still leaves her privileged account exposed while she does routine work. B: she needs the rights for her security duties. C: a shared account would also break accountability.
notes.explanation: NIST's least privilege controls ask that people with access to security functions use non-privileged accounts or roles for non-security functions, to limit exposure.
notes.evidence: use non-privileged accounts or roles, when accessing nonsecurity functions.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, AC-6(2), p. 64

notes.front: What risk does separation of duties reduce, according to NIST's control catalogue?
notes.back: Abuse of privileges people were properly given, and malicious activity by one person acting alone, without colluding with others.
notes.explanation: NIST frames separation of duties as a guard against people abusing privileges they were properly given, not only against outsiders.
notes.evidence: Separation of duties addresses the potential for abuse of authorized privileges and helps to reduce the risk of malevolent activity without collusion.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, AC-5 Separation of Duties, Discussion, p. 63

notes.front: At a small charity, the finance officer can add new suppliers to the payment system and also approve payments to them. Which principle does this break?
notes.back: Separation of duties.
notes.choices:
A) Accountability
B) Separation of duties
C) Non-repudiation
D) Need to know
notes.choicesExplained: A: each action can still be traced to the finance officer. C: nobody is denying an action. D: the problem is combining two business functions, not access to information she does not need.
notes.explanation: NIST's separation of duties control includes dividing mission or business functions among different individuals or roles, so no one person both sets up and pays a supplier.
notes.evidence: Separation of duties includes dividing mission or business functions and support functions among different individuals or roles,
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, AC-5 Separation of Duties, Discussion, p. 63

notes.front: A hospital porter uses a colleague's unlocked workstation to look up a famous patient's records out of curiosity. Nothing is changed. Which security objective has been lost?
notes.back: Confidentiality.
notes.choices:
A) Integrity
B) Availability
C) Confidentiality
D) None, because nothing was changed
notes.choicesExplained: A: no record was modified or destroyed. B: the records stayed available to staff. D: reading without authorisation is itself a loss.
notes.explanation: NIST's security categorisation standard defines a loss of confidentiality as unauthorised disclosure, and the records were disclosed to someone with no authorisation to see them.
notes.evidence: A loss of confidentiality is the unauthorized disclosure of information.
notes.source: FIPS 199, Section 3 Categorization of Information and Information Systems, p. 6

notes.front: A disgruntled clerk deletes last month's delivery records from a shared database without permission. Backups let the records be restored. Under NIST's security categorisation standard, which security objective did the deletion breach?
notes.back: Integrity, because unauthorised destruction counts as a loss of integrity.
notes.choices:
A) Integrity
B) Confidentiality
C) Non-repudiation
D) Accountability
notes.choicesExplained: B: nothing was disclosed to anyone. C: nobody is denying an action they took. D: the deletion may well be traceable to the clerk; the harm is to the records themselves.
notes.explanation: The standard puts destruction, not only modification, under loss of integrity.
notes.evidence: A loss of integrity is the unauthorized modification or destruction of information.
notes.source: FIPS 199, Section 3 Categorization of Information and Information Systems, p. 6

notes.front: A power cut in a council's server room leaves its planning application system unusable for a working day. No data is read or altered. Which security objective has been lost?
notes.back: Availability.
notes.choices:
A) Confidentiality
B) Integrity
C) Accountability
D) Availability
notes.choicesExplained: A: nothing was disclosed. B: nothing was modified or destroyed. C: no action needs tracing to a person; the system simply could not be used.
notes.explanation: NIST's security categorisation standard defines a loss of availability as disruption of access to or use of information or a system, whatever the cause.
notes.evidence: A loss of availability is the disruption of access to or use of information or an information system.
notes.source: FIPS 199, Section 3 Categorization of Information and Information Systems, p. 6

notes.front: During a joint audit, a certified practitioner finds that a certified colleague marked firewall rules as reviewed when he never looked at them, and the client was billed for the work. What does the ISC2 Code expect of her?
notes.back: To follow ISC2's ethics complaint procedure about the colleague's breach.
notes.choices:
A) Stay silent, since the client has not complained
B) Fix the report quietly and say nothing
C) Follow ISC2's ethics complaint procedure
D) Ask the client to file the complaint instead
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: members who observe a breach are obliged to use the complaint procedure, and failing to do so may count as a breach of Canon IV. D: the obligation falls on the member who saw the breach.
notes.explanation: The Code obliges members who see another member breach it to use the complaint procedure; the colleague's false report goes against honest behaviour and careful, capable service to principals.
notes.source: ISC2, Code of Ethics page, “Code” and canons
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A client asks a certified practitioner to leave out of her report a flaw that lets anyone on the internet switch off a town's water pumps, because fixing it would delay a product launch. Which canon speaks most directly to this?
notes.back: Canon I, which covers protecting society, the common good, the trust the public needs, and the infrastructure.
notes.choices:
A) Canon III: give principals careful, capable service
B) Canon IV: help the profession move forward and defend it
C) Canon II: behave honourably, honestly, fairly, responsibly and lawfully
D) Canon I: safeguard society, the public good and the infrastructure
notes.choicesExplained: A: the request comes from the principal, but hiding the flaw endangers the public, which Canon I covers. B: the profession's standing is secondary to the risk to the town. C: honesty is involved, but the harm at stake is to public infrastructure.
notes.explanation: Canon I is the one that names society and the infrastructure, and a public water supply is both.
notes.source: ISC2, Code of Ethics page, “Code of Ethics Canons”
